source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 7 (courseware unit 25): special purpose acquisition companies

facts.statement: SPAC meaning (courseware): a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) has no commercial operations and is incorporated only to raise capital through an initial public offering (IPO) for the purpose of acquiring or merging with an existing company; investors contribute to a fund that will later acquire one or more unnamed enterprises revealed after the IPO. SPACs are also called blank cheque companies. They are formed by sponsors (investors or experienced people in a sector); the sponsor usually has at least one target in mind but it is not disclosed at the IPO, so IPO investors do not know the business they will own. Before the IPO the SPAC gets underwriters and institutional investors. IPO money sits in a trust account that earns interest and may be used only for the acquisition or returned to investors on dissolution (interest may in a few cases fund working capital). After the acquisition the SPAC is normally listed on a stock exchange. Many SPACs fail and investors can lose capital; SPACs compete with venture capital, private equity, direct listing and the traditional IPO. The courseware states that the Indian Companies Act, 2013 does not allow blank cheque companies and that Indian regulators were considering a framework (position as at the courseware date).

Advantages of SPAC over an IPO (courseware): speedier execution (a SPAC merger typically takes about three to six months, an IPO twelve to eighteen); discovery of price up front (negotiated with the SPAC before the transaction, not set by market conditions on the listing day); the possibility of raising additional capital through debt or a PIPE (private investment in public equity), which also backstops redemptions; reduced marketing cost (no full roadshow to public investors, though a PIPE needs its own); ease of access to specialised operational knowledge of the sponsors (experienced business and financial experts with networks); and further benefits: shorter time to become publicly traded, valuation and finance raised together, greater control over the terms, less regulatory oversight and simpler going public of a highly leveraged company.

Disadvantages of SPAC (courseware): inability of the investor to track use of funds (no idea where money will be invested; limited oversight and disclosure); poor returns after the initial hype (the courseware cites a September 2021 study in which the median SPAC underperformed a broad index after the deal closed); low market cap (many trading below the IPO price of $10); increasing regulatory oversight and disclosure norms; shareholding dilution (sponsors typically own 20 per cent of the SPAC through founder shares or promote, plus warrants and possibly an earnout); deficiency in available capital if redemptions are higher than expected, forcing PIPE financing; compact timeframe for compliance (the target prepares audited financials and builds public-company functions in a shorter time than for an IPO); narrower scope of financial due diligence than a traditional IPO, with a risk of restatements; and absence of an underwriter and comfort letter for the target, since the SPAC is already public.

SPAC formation and timeline (courseware): a SPAC is built on an investment thesis for a particular industry and region or the track record of the sponsor. After the IPO, proceeds go to a trust account and the SPAC typically has 18 to 24 months to find and finalise a merger with a target (called the de-SPAC); if it cannot, it is liquidated and the IPO money is distributed to public shareholders. Public shareholders may vote against the deal or redeem their shares; if more funds are needed the SPAC may issue debt or shares in a PIPE or sell assets. The typical life of the vehicle is up to about 24 months from IPO. The merger needs shareholder approval and the filing of a proxy statement or registration statement with financial information about the target (pro forma statements, history, management discussion); once approved and closed, the target becomes a public company and the SPAC is wound up as a separate vehicle.

Stakeholders (courseware): three groups: sponsors, investors and targets. Sponsors start the SPAC and fund its costs (underwriting, attorney and due diligence fees) with non-refundable capital, about $7 to $8 million in the courseware example of a $500 million SPAC; if no combination happens within the period (two years in the courseware text), the SPAC is dissolved and sponsors lose the risk capital, whereas if the deal completes they receive founder shares worth about 20 per cent of the equity raised. Example in the courseware: the SPAC sells 50 million units at $10 and the sponsor buys about 12.5 million founder shares (20 per cent of all outstanding shares) at a nominal price; if the merger is completed and the share vests at $10 the founder stake is worth $125 million. Sponsors must have a strong concept, attract investors, find a suitable target and convince both that the combination has financial and strategic benefit; competition among SPACs for targets and investors raises the chance that a sponsor loses the capital and time invested. Investors can sell, hold or redeem; targets are private companies seeking to go public.

Characteristics of SPACs (courseware): after the IPO a SPAC may trade as units, or as separate common shares and warrants, so investors can easily exit; the corporation must give target-business stockholders full disclosure, including audited financial statements and the terms of the proposed combination, so that shareholders can make an informed decision, and all stakeholders have voting rights at the shareholder meeting. The SPAC is led by an experienced management team of at least three people with a background in private equity, mergers and acquisitions or operating roles; the team is entitled to about 20 per cent of the equity of the vehicle, excluding any warrants; before the business combination, management receives no cash compensation, finder fee or other cash payment, and if no combination is completed it does not take part in the distribution of the liquidated assets.

SPAC process and sponsor economics (courseware): the sponsors (founders) provide the initial money and pay a minimal price for a portion of the stock; the management team engages an investment bank to run the IPO, which charges a fee of about 10 per cent of IPO value (courseware indication). If more funding is needed, sponsors may lend to the SPAC. The prospectus gives more weight to the investors because the SPAC has no history. IPO money goes into a trust account until a target is chosen; the management team has 18 to 24 months to close an acquisition, and the target enterprise value should typically be at least 80 per cent of the trust assets. To finance part of the price the SPAC organises debt or equity financing such as a PIPE before signing the agreement, announces the deal, and then either runs a tender offer or holds a mandatory shareholder vote; in either case investors have the right to return their shares for cash roughly equal to the IPO price (their share of the trust). If the deal fails within the allotted time, trust funds go back to investors; management is not allowed to collect salary before the deal is final. When the conditions are met the combination forms a publicly traded operating company.

Capital structure and trust account (courseware): a SPAC raises money by an IPO of units, each unit containing a share of common stock and a warrant to buy more shares later; after the IPO the units can be split into separate warrants and common shares that trade in the open market. Typical shareholding after the IPO: public shares 80 per cent and founder shares 20 per cent. The trust account holds an amount equal to or greater than 100 per cent of the gross IPO proceeds (courseware indication: about 95 per cent from the public and 5 per cent from the sponsors), invested in short-term government securities or kept as cash, to pay for the business combination, redemption of common stock under a compulsory redemption offer, the deferred underwriting discount, transaction costs and working capital of the company after the de-SPAC.

Warrants and forward purchase (courseware): warrants give the right to buy shares at a strike price; the sponsor buys founder warrants in full, while the units sold to the public usually include only part of a warrant (half a warrant is standard, one third is common in larger IPOs). The strike price is usually based on the share price at the IPO. Public warrants are typically settled in cash (the holder pays the strike price for a share), whereas founder warrants are net settled (the holder receives shares worth the difference between the trading price and the strike price instead of paying cash). Public warrants may be net settled if there is no effective registration statement or at management discretion. If public warrants are exercisable and the shares trade above a fixed price for a set time, the company can redeem the public warrants, forcing holders to exercise or lose them; founder warrants cannot be redeemed for cash. A forward purchase is an agreement by sponsor affiliates or institutional investors to buy equity of the SPAC alongside the de-SPAC to the extent more funds are needed; it may be conditioned on the transaction meeting the investor mandate.

IPO agreements (courseware): documents specific to a SPAC include the charter (sets out the public and founder shares, an anti-dilution adjustment to the founder shares conversion, and limits use of trust money to repurchase of public shares and to a business combination of a minimum size); the securities purchase agreement (the sponsor buys founder shares; the founder shares are typically 25 per cent of the public shares, which equals 20 per cent of the total, and can be adjusted by stock split or forfeiture); the warrant agreement (with the transfer agent; the SPAC must register shares issued on exercise; changing the terms needs approval of fifty per cent of holders); the promissory note (the sponsor lends the SPAC funds for offering costs before the IPO); the sponsor constituent document (the sponsor entity records the participation of its owners); the letter agreement (officers, directors and sponsor agree to lock-up, waive claims against the trust account, vote in favour of the de-SPAC and forfeit founder shares if the over-allotment option is not exercised in full); the registration rights agreement; the private placement warrants purchase agreement (the sponsor buys warrants, with the financing one business day before the IPO closes and before the over-allotment option closes); the securities assignment agreement (independent directors are compensated by a cost-plus sale of founder shares, not fees); the administrative service agreement (a monthly charge to the sponsor for office space and support); and the investment management trust agreement with the trustee controlling investment and release of trust funds.

De-SPAC process (courseware): the steps are shareholder approval (similar to a merger of two public companies, but the SPAC as buyer needs shareholder approval while the target does not need stock exchange shareholders to vote on it in the same way), founder approbation votes, disclosure of material in a super 8-K form, and the redemption offer. Founder vote: founders commit to vote in favour of the de-SPAC with their founder shares and any public shares they hold, so, with founders holding 20 per cent of the shares, only 37.5 per cent of the public shares are needed to carry a majority. Redemption: public holders can exchange their shares for a proportionate share of the trust account; public warrants, founder shares and founder warrants have no redemption right; if the time limit passes and the charter is not changed to extend it, the SPAC must redeem the public shares for their share of the trust, the money is returned and the public warrants, founder shares and founder warrants lose their value and expire.

payload.title: What a SPAC is
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **special purpose acquisition company (SPAC)** has **no commercial operations**. It is formed only to **raise money in an IPO** and then **acquire or merge with an existing company**. It is also called a **blank cheque company**: investors do not know the **target** at the IPO.

- **Sponsors** (experienced investors) form it; they usually have **a target in mind but do not disclose it**.
- IPO money sits in a **trust account**, may be used **only for the acquisition**, or is **returned on dissolution**.
- After the acquisition the combined company is normally **listed**.
- **Risk:** many SPACs fail; investors can lose money. SPACs compete with **private equity, venture capital, direct listings and the conventional IPO**.
- The courseware states that the **Companies Act, 2013 does not allow blank cheque companies** in India and that a framework was under consideration (position at the courseware date).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Investors back the sponsors track record because there is no business to assess.

payload.title: SPAC formation and timeline
payload.core_explanation_md:
A SPAC is built on an **investment thesis** (industry and region) or the **sponsor track record**.

1. **IPO**: proceeds go into a **trust account**.
2. **Search**: typically **18 to 24 months** to find and finalise a merger (the **de-SPAC**).
3. **Vote**: public shareholders may **vote against** or **redeem**; extra money may come from a **PIPE** (debt or shares) or asset sales.
4. **Approval and closing**: proxy or registration statement with **pro forma financials**; the **target becomes public**.
5. **If no deal**: the SPAC is **liquidated** and IPO money is **distributed** to public holders.

payload.title: Stakeholders: sponsors, investors and targets
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Stakeholder | Role and economics |
| --- | --- |
| **Sponsors** | Start the SPAC and pay its costs with **non-refundable risk capital**; **lose it if no deal**; if the deal closes, get **founder shares of about 20 per cent** |
| **Investors** | Buy units; may **sell, hold or redeem**; have **voting rights** at the shareholder meeting |
| **Targets** | **Private companies** seeking to go public |

**Management team:** at least **three experienced people** (private equity, M&A, operating); about **20 per cent of the equity** (excluding warrants); **no cash pay, finder fee or other cash** before the deal; **no share of liquidation** if no deal.

**Disclosure:** the SPAC must give the target stockholders **audited financials and the terms** of the combination.

payload.title: The SPAC process step by step
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. **Founders** put in initial money for a **nominal price**.
2. An **investment bank** runs the IPO (courseware indication of fee: **about 10 per cent**).
3. Proceeds go to a **trust account**; the **prospectus focuses on the investors** because the SPAC has no history.
4. The team has **18 to 24 months** to find a target whose **enterprise value is typically at least 80 per cent of the trust assets**.
5. **Financing**: a **PIPE** or debt is arranged **before signing**; **sponsors** may lend.
6. **Announcement**, then a **tender offer** or **mandatory shareholder vote**; investors can **return shares for cash roughly equal to the IPO price**.
7. **Closing**: a **publicly traded operating company** results. If no deal, **trust funds return to investors**; no salary before the deal is final.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 80 per cent test ensures the target is large enough to justify the vehicle.

self_check.prompt_text: Roughly what share of the trust assets should the target enterprise value represent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least 80 per cent.

payload.title: Founder share arithmetic and the approval threshold
payload.core_explanation_md:
Founder shares **F** and public shares **P**:

- **Founder stake = F / (F + P)**; **F = P x 0.25** gives **20 per cent** of the total.
- **Founder value = F x share price.**
- **Votes needed from public holders for a majority of all shares = (0.5 x (F + P) - F) / P**, if founders vote in favour with all their shares.

Example: **P = 50 million**, **F = 12.5 million**, price **$10**: stake **20 per cent**; value **$125 million**; threshold **(31.25 - 12.5) / 50 = 37.5 per cent** of public shares.

assumptions: Founders vote in favour with all their shares
common_errors: Dividing F by P instead of by F + P
Forgetting the founders own votes in the threshold

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Founder votes cut the share of public votes needed to approve a deal.

payload.title: Capital structure and the trust account
payload.core_explanation_md:
The IPO sells **units**: each has **one share of common stock and a warrant (or part of one)**. After the IPO they can be **split** and traded separately.

**Shareholding after IPO (courseware): public 80 per cent, founders 20 per cent.**

**Trust account:** **at least 100 per cent of gross IPO proceeds** (courseware indication: about **95 per cent from the public and 5 per cent from sponsors**), held in **short-term government securities or cash**. Uses: **the business combination**, **redemption of shares**, the **deferred underwriting discount**, **transaction costs** and **working capital** after the de-SPAC.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The trust protects public money until a deal is approved.

self_check.prompt_text: Where are SPAC IPO proceeds held?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In a trust account, invested in short-term government securities or kept as cash.

payload.title: Warrants and forward purchase
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **warrant** gives the right to buy a share at a **strike price**, usually based on the **IPO share price**.

| | Public warrants | Founder warrants |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Held by** | Public unit holders (often **half a warrant** per unit; **one third** in larger IPOs) | **Sponsor** (bought in full) |
| **Exercise** | Usually **cash settled**: pay the strike | **Net settled**: receive shares worth **(price - strike)** |
| **Redemption** | **Company can redeem** if the share price stays above a set level: holders must **exercise or lose** them | **Cannot be redeemed for cash** |

**Forward purchase:** sponsor affiliates or institutions agree to **buy equity** alongside the de-SPAC if more funds are needed; may depend on the **investor mandate**.

**Net settlement shares = warrants x (price - strike) / price.**
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Net settlement saves the sponsor from paying cash to exercise.

self_check.prompt_text: How does net settlement of founder warrants work?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The holder receives shares worth the trading price less the strike price instead of paying cash.

payload.core_explanation_md:

| **Securities purchase agreement** | **Sponsor buys founder shares**: **25 per cent of public shares = 20 per cent of the total** |
| **Warrant agreement** | Terms with the transfer agent; change needs **50 per cent of holders** |

payload.title: The de-SPAC process: approval, founder votes and redemption
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** **shareholder approval**, **founder approbation votes**, **disclosure in a super 8-K** (US form named by the courseware) and the **redemption offer**.

- **Approval:** like a merger of two public companies, but it is the **SPAC (buyer)** that needs its shareholders approval.
- **Founder vote:** founders commit to **vote in favour** with founder shares and any public shares; with founders at **20 per cent**, only about **37.5 per cent of public shares** are needed for a majority.
- **Redemption:** public holders can **exchange shares for a proportionate share of the trust**. Public **warrants**, **founder shares** and **founder warrants** have **no redemption right**.
- **Time limit:** if the deadline passes and the charter is **not extended**, the SPAC must **redeem public shares**; public warrants, founder shares and founder warrants **expire worthless**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Redemption lets a public holder leave with the trust value if it dislikes the deal.

self_check.expected_takeaway: They lose their value and expire.

items.title: What a SPAC is
items.core_explanation_md:
A **special purpose acquisition company (SPAC)** has **no commercial operations**. It is formed only to **raise money in an IPO** and then **acquire or merge with an existing company**. It is also called a **blank cheque company**: investors do not know the **target** at the IPO.

- **Sponsors** (experienced investors) form it; they usually have **a target in mind but do not disclose it**.
- IPO money sits in a **trust account**, may be used **only for the acquisition**, or is **returned on dissolution**.
- After the acquisition the combined company is normally **listed**.
- **Risk:** many SPACs fail; investors can lose money. SPACs compete with **private equity, venture capital, direct listings and the conventional IPO**.
- The courseware states that the **Companies Act, 2013 does not allow blank cheque companies** in India and that a framework was under consideration (position at the courseware date).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Investors back the sponsors track record because there is no business to assess.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Investors give money without knowing which business it will buy.

items.title: Advantages of a SPAC merger over an IPO
items.core_explanation_md:
| Advantage | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Speed** | About **3 to 6 months** against **12 to 18** for an IPO |
| **Price certainty** | Price is **negotiated up front**, not set by the market on listing day |
| **Extra capital** | **Debt or a PIPE** (private investment in public equity) can be raised, and **backstops redemptions** |
| **Lower marketing cost** | No full public roadshow |
| **Sponsor expertise** | Experienced business and financial people and their networks |

Others: **shorter time to go public**, **valuation and funding together**, **more control over terms**, **less regulatory oversight**, easier for a **highly leveraged** company.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Fixing the price before the transaction removes the risk of a poor market on IPO day.

items.title: Disadvantages of a SPAC
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Investor cannot track the use of funds**; little oversight and disclosure.
- **Poor returns** after the hype fades; many trade **below the IPO price** (courseware illustration).
- **Rising regulation and disclosure norms**.
- **Dilution**: sponsors typically hold **20 per cent** through **founder shares (the promote)**, plus **warrants** and possibly an **earnout**.
- **Capital shortfall** if **redemptions** are higher than expected, forcing **PIPE** funding.
- **Short timeframe** for the target to prepare **audited financials** and build **public-company functions**.
- **Narrower due diligence** than a traditional IPO: risk of **restatement** or wrong valuation.
- **No underwriter or comfort letter** for the target, since the SPAC is already public.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Founder shares are bought at a nominal price, so they dilute the public holders.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The SPAC is already public, so the underwriter role of a traditional IPO is absent.

items.title: SPAC formation and timeline
items.core_explanation_md:
A SPAC is built on an **investment thesis** (industry and region) or the **sponsor track record**.

1. **IPO**: proceeds go into a **trust account**.
2. **Search**: typically **18 to 24 months** to find and finalise a merger (the **de-SPAC**).
3. **Vote**: public shareholders may **vote against** or **redeem**; extra money may come from a **PIPE** (debt or shares) or asset sales.
4. **Approval and closing**: proxy or registration statement with **pro forma financials**; the **target becomes public**.
5. **If no deal**: the SPAC is **liquidated** and IPO money is **distributed** to public holders.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The deadline forces the sponsor to complete a deal or return the money.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It is liquidated and the IPO money is distributed to public shareholders.

items.core_explanation_md:

| --- | --- |
| **Sponsors** | Start the SPAC and pay its costs with **non-refundable risk capital**; **lose it if no deal**; if the deal closes, get **founder shares of about 20 per cent** |
| **Investors** | Buy units; may **sell, hold or redeem**; have **voting rights** at the shareholder meeting |

items.title: The SPAC process step by step
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **Founders** put in initial money for a **nominal price**.
2. An **investment bank** runs the IPO (courseware indication of fee: **about 10 per cent**).
3. Proceeds go to a **trust account**; the **prospectus focuses on the investors** because the SPAC has no history.
4. The team has **18 to 24 months** to find a target whose **enterprise value is typically at least 80 per cent of the trust assets**.
5. **Financing**: a **PIPE** or debt is arranged **before signing**; **sponsors** may lend.
6. **Announcement**, then a **tender offer** or **mandatory shareholder vote**; investors can **return shares for cash roughly equal to the IPO price**.
7. **Closing**: a **publicly traded operating company** results. If no deal, **trust funds return to investors**; no salary before the deal is final.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 80 per cent test ensures the target is large enough to justify the vehicle.

self_check.expected_takeaway: At least 80 per cent.

items.title: Founder share arithmetic and the approval threshold
items.core_explanation_md:
Founder shares **F** and public shares **P**:

- **Founder stake = F / (F + P)**; **F = P x 0.25** gives **20 per cent** of the total.
- **Founder value = F x share price.**
- **Votes needed from public holders for a majority of all shares = (0.5 x (F + P) - F) / P**, if founders vote in favour with all their shares.

Example: **P = 50 million**, **F = 12.5 million**, price **$10**: stake **20 per cent**; value **$125 million**; threshold **(31.25 - 12.5) / 50 = 37.5 per cent** of public shares.

assumptions: Founders vote in favour with all their shares
common_errors: Dividing F by P instead of by F + P
Forgetting the founders own votes in the threshold

items.title: Capital structure and the trust account
items.core_explanation_md:
The IPO sells **units**: each has **one share of common stock and a warrant (or part of one)**. After the IPO they can be **split** and traded separately.

**Trust account:** **at least 100 per cent of gross IPO proceeds** (courseware indication: about **95 per cent from the public and 5 per cent from sponsors**), held in **short-term government securities or cash**. Uses: **the business combination**, **redemption of shares**, the **deferred underwriting discount**, **transaction costs** and **working capital** after the de-SPAC.

items.title: Warrants and forward purchase
items.core_explanation_md:
A **warrant** gives the right to buy a share at a **strike price**, usually based on the **IPO share price**.

| | Public warrants | Founder warrants |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Held by** | Public unit holders (often **half a warrant** per unit; **one third** in larger IPOs) | **Sponsor** (bought in full) |
| **Exercise** | Usually **cash settled**: pay the strike | **Net settled**: receive shares worth **(price - strike)** |
| **Redemption** | **Company can redeem** if the share price stays above a set level: holders must **exercise or lose** them | **Cannot be redeemed for cash** |

**Forward purchase:** sponsor affiliates or institutions agree to **buy equity** alongside the de-SPAC if more funds are needed; may depend on the **investor mandate**.

**Net settlement shares = warrants x (price - strike) / price.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: Net settlement saves the sponsor from paying cash to exercise.

items.title: The de-SPAC process: approval, founder votes and redemption
items.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** **shareholder approval**, **founder approbation votes**, **disclosure in a super 8-K** (US form named by the courseware) and the **redemption offer**.

- **Approval:** like a merger of two public companies, but it is the **SPAC (buyer)** that needs its shareholders approval.
- **Founder vote:** founders commit to **vote in favour** with founder shares and any public shares; with founders at **20 per cent**, only about **37.5 per cent of public shares** are needed for a majority.
- **Redemption:** public holders can **exchange shares for a proportionate share of the trust**. Public **warrants**, **founder shares** and **founder warrants** have **no redemption right**.
- **Time limit:** if the deadline passes and the charter is **not extended**, the SPAC must **redeem public shares**; public warrants, founder shares and founder warrants **expire worthless**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Redemption lets a public holder leave with the trust value if it dislikes the deal.
